newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Telecom likely target for U.S. rate plan.
newsitem.headline: HK Telecom likely target for U.S. rate plan.

text.p: Hongkong Telecommunications Ltd is likely to feel the brunt of Washington's efforts to force down international calling rates whatever the validity of the company's arguments against U.S. regulators, analysts say.
But they said lower settlement rates could hurt Hongkong Telecom's new and rapidly growing rivals even more.

"Because they're at an earlier stage of development, and most of these new operators rely to a substantial extent on international delivery fees for their revenue streams, I think they will be very significantly affected, negatively affected," said Lloyd Fischer, regional telecom analyst at BZW Asia.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposed in December to cap settlement rates -- fees carriers pay each other to complete calls -- for U.S.-originated calls at 15, 19 and 23 U.S. cents per minute for high, middle and low-income countries.
The FCC argued that while the average cost to complete a call is no more than nine cents, settlement rates now tend to be five to 10 times costs, forcing U.S. callers to pay too much.

Hongkong Telecom is likely to be targeted as one of the largest net receivers of settlement fees but also because it has an extremely developed market, a high settlement rate and a monopoly on international voice calls, analysts say.
"If I was the FCC and wanted to make a point, Hong Kong is one of the markets I would focus on," said David Gibbons, regional telecoms analyst at HSBC James Capel.
More calls originate in the United States than terminate there, by a ratio of seven-to-one in the case of Hong Kong, so U.S. carriers pay more settlement fees than they get back.
The outflow is expected to hit US$5.5 billion in 1996, the FCC said.
Comments on the FCC proposal are due by February 7, and Hongkong Telecom has pledged to file strong objections.

The company argues the growing imbalance in U.S.-originated to U.S.-destined calls is a recent phenomenon created by the growth of "call-back" services, which bounce back U.S.-destined calls as U.S.-originated calls and charge U.S. rates.
In the year to March 31, Hongkong Telecom is forecast to receive at least US$200 million more from U.S. carriers than it will pay.
Analysts agreed with Hongkong Telecom that the FCC had aided the growth of call-back operators and that much of the benefit of lower settlement fees would flow to U.S. carriers.
If the U.S.-Hong Kong settlement rate dropped to the FCC proposed 15 cents a minute from 47 cents at present, Hongkong Telecom would get drastically lower fees from U.S. carriers.
Since costs are unaffected, the loss would come mostly from profits.
Theoretically, lower settlement fees could make call-back services more popular -- a further blow to Asian telecom carriers.
"Lower settlement fees means lower call-back charges, so it makes it much harder to maintain your outgoing tariff rates," Fischer said.
But under Hong Kong's complex market-opening policy, much of the pain will be shared out between Hongkong Telecom's three new rivals.
Hutchison Telecom, New World Telecom and New T&T were allowed to enter the fixed-line market in 1995 when Hongkong Telecom's monopoly was ended.

Hongkong Telecom still has a theoretical lock on cross-border calls and the newcomers must route international traffic through the company's lines, but their use of call-back has undercut Hongkong Telecom's prices and grabbed market share.
Hongkong Telecom says it has lost 15 percent of the international market to the three new competitors and other call-back operators despite its monopoly.

Hongkong Telecom also pays a delivery fee of 29 cents a minute to the newcomers for international calls they complete, an arrangement designed to help fund development of the domestic networks of Hutchison Telecom, New World Telecom and New T&T.
But if Hong Kong regulators slash the delivery fees Hongkong Telecom pays in line with lower settlement fees it might receive from abroad, then much of that extra money will disappear.

"I think it's fair to say that overall the scenario will probably be negative for the other operators. At the moment, there is no doubt that the (settlement fee) surplus is de facto providing a subsidy to the operators," Gibbons said.
No one will come out unscathed. Hongkong Telecom's profits might take a four percent hit, but that is better than the 14 percent hit the firm would take without the delivery fee agreement.
And none of this will happen overnight, analysts emphasise.
The FCC will decide on its policy by mid-year at the earliest, after which carriers will have at least one year to negotiate.
